title: Mirik Lake, Bokar Monastery and the Tea Road
meta_description: A practical guide to Mirik: walking Sumendu Lake, boats and prices, Bokar monastery, the Tingling and Sourenee tea viewpoints, where to stay and when to go.
summary: Mirik is a small lake town at about 1,495 m, 52 km from Siliguri, built around Sumendu Lake, which opened in 1979. Walk the 3.5 km lake road, climb to Bokar monastery, founded in 1984, and stop at Tingling and Sourenee tea gardens on the way. Budget doubles start at about ₹1,200; one or two nights is enough.

sections.heading: Mirik in brief
paras: Mirik sits in a bowl of hills on the western side of the Darjeeling hills, at about 1,495 m, with tea estates on the slopes all around and the Nepal border a few ridges to the west. It is roughly the same height as Kurseong and noticeably warmer and calmer than Darjeeling. The town has two halves: the main bazaar and jeep stand on one side of the lake, and Krishnanagar, where most hotels are, on the other. Above both, Bokar monastery looks down from the hill.

It is the easiest place in this land for a relaxed family trip. There are no steep climbs to the main sights, the lake walk is level, food is easy to find, and the drive up from Siliguri passes through some of the most photographed tea country in the hills. Mirik had 11,363 residents at the 2011 census, and outside festival weekends it feels like the small town it is.

A simple day here looks like this: the lake walk at dawn, breakfast in the bazaar, a slow climb to Bokar monastery mid-morning, lunch of momos or a thali, an afternoon on the Krishnanagar side or a short car trip to the tea gardens, and an early night. Mirik goes quiet by 8 pm, so eat dinner early or at your hotel. If you want more walking, the estate roads below town lead through tea and small villages; ask your hotel for a route and carry water.

sections.heading: The story of the lake and the name
paras: The name Mirik comes from the Lepcha Mir-Yok, usually translated as 'place burnt by fire', which may remember an old clearing of forest by burning for fields. For a long time the valley bottom was marsh, with tea estates such as Thurbo, Sourenee and Gopaldhara planted on the surrounding slopes from the late nineteenth century and orange orchards in the warmer pockets below.

In 1974 work began to turn the marsh into a lake as part of a plan to create a new hill resort, and Sumendu Lake was opened in April 1979, with a 3.5 km road around it and a footbridge across the water. Hotels followed at Krishnanagar. In 1984 the Tibetan teacher Bokar Rinpoche (1940–2004), a master of the Kagyu tradition, founded a small retreat centre on the hill above the town. As students asked to join him, it grew into Bokar Ngedhon Chokhorling, the monastery that now overlooks Mirik.

sections.heading: Walking and boating on Sumendu Lake
paras: The lake is a little over a kilometre long, with tall Japanese cedars along one bank and gardens on the other. The 3.5 km road around it is mostly level and takes about an hour at an easy pace, longer if you stop for tea and photographs. Start early: from 6 to 8 am the water is still, the mist lifts off the surface, and the paths belong to locals on their morning walks. By late morning on weekends the bazaar end is crowded with families and pony handlers.

Rowing boats cost about ₹150–300 for roughly 20 minutes, and pony rides along the lake road are priced by distance; agree the price first. Neither is needed to enjoy the lake. Cross the footbridge for the view back over the water, and walk the Krishnanagar side in the afternoon, when the light comes across the hills. In the monsoon the lake path can be slippery, and some boats stop running in heavy rain.

sections.heading: Bokar monastery
paras: Bokar monastery stands on the hill above the lake, about a 20–30 minute walk uphill from the bazaar, or a short taxi ride. It belongs to the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism and has a main prayer hall, a large stupa, residential buildings for monks and a retreat centre where practitioners have traditionally undertaken long retreats. The prayer wheels along the path and the view down over Mirik's bowl of hills make the climb worthwhile even if you do not go inside.

Visitors are welcome in daylight. Walk clockwise around the stupa and prayer wheels, take off your shoes before entering a hall, keep your voice low, and ask before photographing monks or the inside of the halls. Morning and evening prayers can sometimes be heard from outside. Losar, the Tibetan New Year in February or March, is the main festival here; dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. A small donation is welcome but not required. If you visit with children, explain beforehand that the monastery is a working place of study and prayer, not a park.

sections.heading: The tea road: Tingling, Sourenee and Gopaldhara
paras: The road up from Siliguri is half the reason to come. After crossing the Balason river at Dudhia, it climbs through the tea estates of Tingling and Sourenee, where the bushes run in long curves along the contours and the land falls away towards the Mechi valley and Nepal. Tingling's viewpoint is simply a wide bend in the road with tea stalls; drivers on reserved cars will usually stop for a few minutes without extra charge. Sourenee, about 7 km below Mirik, has a recorded history unusual in Darjeeling: a Nepali sardar named Dakman Rai received the land, his son Bhoujit planted the first tea, and the Tiwari brothers formally established the estate in 1902.

On the other side of Mirik, the road towards Darjeeling passes Gopaldhara, one of the highest gardens in the district, with sections between about 1,700 and 2,100 m. Ask for a stop there on a transfer to Darjeeling, or hire a car from Mirik for a half day for about ₹1,200–1,800.

sections.heading: Where to stay and how long
paras: Krishnanagar, across the lake from the bazaar, has most of Mirik's hotels, from small budget places at about ₹1,200–2,500 a double to larger family hotels. The bazaar side is closer to the jeep stand and food stalls but noisier. For space and quiet, the GTA-run Swiss Cottages sit on the high ground above the lake; confirm the booking channel and current operation before you go. For a more local stay, homestays in the villages and tea estates around Mirik charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals; ask in Mirik for current names.

One night is enough to walk the lake, climb to the monastery and see the tea road. Two nights let you go slowly, add Gopaldhara and spend a morning on the estate paths around Sourenee. Mirik pairs well with Darjeeling, about 2 hours away, or with Kurseong, which is better reached by car.
list: Walk the lake road at dawn, before the crowds
Climb to Bokar monastery in the late afternoon for the light
Ask your jeep or car to stop at Tingling on the way up
Avoid arriving unbooked on Puja and long weekends

faqs.a: Yes, for a calm night or two. Mirik is a small, easy town around Sumendu Lake, with a level 3.5 km lake walk, Bokar monastery on the hill above and tea gardens all around. The drive up from Siliguri through Tingling and Sourenee is one of the best tea landscapes in the hills. It is quieter and cheaper than Darjeeling outside festival weekends.

faqs.q: How long is the walk around Mirik lake?
faqs.a: The road around Sumendu Lake is about 3.5 km and mostly level, taking about an hour at an easy pace. Cross the footbridge for a view back over the water. Early morning, between 6 and 8 am, is the quietest and most beautiful time. The path can be slippery in the monsoon, so wear shoes with grip.

faqs.q: How much does boating cost in Mirik lake?
faqs.a: A rowing boat costs about ₹150–300 for around 20 minutes, depending on the season and the boat. Pony rides along the lake road are charged by distance; agree the price before you start. Rates are indicative and may change, so check at the boat stand. Boats may stop in heavy rain.

Yes. Visitors are welcome in daylight at Bokar Ngedhon Chokhorling, the Kagyu monastery above Mirik. Take off your shoes before entering a prayer hall, walk clockwise around the stupa and prayer wheels, keep quiet, and ask before photographing monks or the interior. The walk up from the bazaar takes about 20–30 minutes. A small donation is welcome.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Mirik?
faqs.a: One night is enough to walk the lake, visit Bokar monastery and stop at Tingling and Sourenee on the way up. Two nights allow a slower pace and a half-day trip to Gopaldhara or the estate paths. Many travellers pair Mirik with Darjeeling, about two hours away by shared jeep, or with a night in Kurseong.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Mirik on a budget?
faqs.a: Krishnanagar, on the far side of the lake from the bazaar, has the most budget hotels, with doubles from about ₹1,200–2,500. The bazaar side is handy for jeeps but noisier. Village homestays around the tea estates charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals. Book ahead for Durga Puja, Christmas and May weekends.

Not in its present form. The valley bottom was a marsh until 1974, when work began to turn it into a lake as part of a plan for a new hill resort. Sumendu Lake was opened in April 1979 with a 3.5 km road around it and a footbridge. Hotels then grew up at Krishnanagar on the far shore, and the lake became the centre of the town.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mirik?
faqs.a: October to December and March to May are best. Autumn and early winter bring clear air and orange season in the warmer villages, while spring brings first flush tea and fresh green. May and Durga Puja weeks are the busiest. From late June to September, rain is heavy, views are rare and the Dudhia road can be slowed by landslides.

faqs.q: How far is Mirik from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 49 km by the road through Sukhia Pokhari and Simana, taking around 2 hours. Shared jeeps cost about ₹150–200 a seat, with fewer departures after early afternoon, and a reserved car costs about ₹2,500–3,200. On the way you can stop at Gopaldhara tea estate, one of the highest gardens in the Darjeeling hills.
